title: Reactions of acids
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.4.2-c01, 4.4.2-c38, 4.4.2-c37, 4.4.2-c35. Clues: 4.4.2-c01 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c38 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c37 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c35 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.4.2-q23, 4.4.2-q29, 4.4.2-q24, 4.4.2-q30, 4.4.2-q25, 4.4.2-q31, 4.4.2-q26, 4.4.2-q32, 4.4.2-q27, 4.4.2-q28, 4.4.2-q33, 4.4.2-q36, 4.4.2-q34, 4.4.2-q37, 4.4.2-q35, 4.4.2-q38.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Salt
items.clue: A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or by another positive ion.

items.label: End point
items.clue: The moment when the indicator changes colour permanently, showing that the acid and alkali have exactly reacted.

items.label: Pipette
items.clue: Apparatus that delivers an accurate fixed volume, used with a safety filler to place the alkali in the conical flask.

items.label: Titration
items.clue: A method of measuring the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.

questions.stem: Which ion do all acids produce in aqueous solution?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
Chloride ions, Cl⁻
Oxide ions, O²⁻
Hydrogen ions, H⁺

questions.explanation: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solutions; this is what makes a solution acidic.

questions.stem: What is measured in a titration between an acid and an alkali?

options.text: The mass of salt made when they are mixed
The temperature rise during the reaction
The exact pH at every stage of the reaction
The volumes of the solutions that react together

questions.explanation: Titration measures the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.

questions.stem: What do aqueous solutions of alkalis contain?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
The hydrogen ions, H⁺
Hydrogen molecules, H₂
Water molecules only

questions.explanation: Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, OH⁻, which is why they neutralise acids.

questions.stem: In a titration, how should the 25.0 cm³ of alkali be measured into the conical flask?

options.text: With a pipette and a safety filler
With a measuring cylinder poured in
From the burette holding the acid
By weighing it out on a balance

questions.explanation: A pipette delivers an accurate, fixed volume of alkali into the flask, and a filler is used instead of mouth suction.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?

options.text: It runs from 1 to 14 and measures the acid strength
It runs from 0 to 7 for acids and no further
It runs from 0 to 14 and measures acidity or alkalinity
It runs from 0 to 14 and measures concentration

questions.explanation: The pH scale, from 0 to 14, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution.

questions.stem: Why is a single indicator such as phenolphthalein used in a titration rather than universal indicator?

options.text: It shows the pH at every stage of the titration
It changes colour sharply at the end point
Universal indicator reacts with the acid used
It makes the neutralisation happen faster

questions.explanation: A single indicator gives one sudden colour change, so the end point can be judged to the nearest drop.

questions.stem: Four solutions have pH values of 2, 7, 9 and 13. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The solution at pH 2 must be alkaline and pH 13 acidic
The solution at pH 7 does not contain any ions
The solutions at pH 9 and pH 13 are both neutral
The solution at pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 is alkaline

questions.explanation: Solutions with a pH below 7 are acidic and those above 7 are alkaline, so pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 alkaline.

questions.stem: In Required practical 2, a student records titres of 24.10, 23.55 and 23.60 cm³. What should be done next?

options.text: Take the mean of all three titres recorded
Use the largest titre, because it is safest
Average the two concordant titres only
Repeat until the titres are all identical

questions.explanation: The rough first titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the titres that agree within 0.10 cm³.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?

options.text: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O₂
2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → H₂O
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂

questions.explanation: In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water.

questions.stem: A few drops of universal indicator are added to a solution and the colour is matched to a chart. What does this give?

options.text: An exact pH value, correct to two decimal places
An approximate value for the solution's pH
The concentration of the acid in mol per dm³
The volume of alkali needed for neutralisation

questions.explanation: Universal indicator, a wide range indicator, gives an approximate pH when its colour is matched to a chart.

questions.stem: (HT) How many moles are there in 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³?

options.text: 2.00 mol
200 mol

questions.explanation: The volume in dm³ is 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0200 dm³, so moles = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol.

questions.stem: (HT) What does it mean to say that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?

options.text: It contains a large amount of acid in each dm³
It is no more ionised than a weak acid is
It will react with every metal that is added to it
It is completely ionised in aqueous solution

questions.explanation: A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so every acid molecule releases its hydrogen ion.

questions.stem: (HT) 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, reacting 1:1. What is the concentration of the alkali?

options.text: 0.00800 mol/dm³
0.0800 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
0.05 mol/dm³

questions.explanation: Moles of acid = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol, so moles of alkali = 0.00200 mol and 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

questions.stem: (HT) Which set contains only weak acids?

options.text: Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids
Ethanoic acid, citric acid and carbonic acid
Ethanoic acid, nitric and sulfuric acids
Citric acid, carbonic acid and nitric acid

questions.explanation: Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are the weak acids named in the specification; each is only partially ionised.

questions.stem: (HT) A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is this in g/dm³? (Mᵣ of NaOH = 40)

options.text: 0.002 g/dm³
0.08 g/dm³
3.2 g/dm³
32 g/dm³

questions.explanation: Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mᵣ = 0.0800 × 40 = 3.2 g/dm³.

questions.stem: (HT) A bottle is labelled 'concentrated ethanoic acid'. What does the word concentrated tell you?

options.text: The ethanoic acid in it is completely ionised
There is only a little acid dissolved in each dm³
A large amount of acid is dissolved in each dm³
It cannot be a weak acid when concentrated

questions.explanation: Concentrated describes the amount of substance dissolved in a given volume; ethanoic acid is still a weak acid.
